solution:
\(\mathrm{HCl}\) is a strong acid, so it dissociates completely and contributes \(10^{-8}\) mol dm\(^{-3}\) of \(\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}\). That is one-tenth of what water itself supplies, so at this dilution the autoionisation of water can no longer be ignored.

Writing \(x = [\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}]\), the charge balance gives \(x = 10^{-8} + K_w/x\), that is \(x^2 - 10^{-8}x - 10^{-14} = 0\), whose positive root is \(x = 1.05 \times 10^{-7}\) mol dm\(^{-3}\). Hence pH \(= -\log_{10}(1.05 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.98\), which is less than 7.

Testing the other options: 8 is what the formula \(-\log_{10}(10^{-8})\) returns if the water equilibrium is ignored, but a pH of 8 means the solution is BASIC, and adding an acid to water can never make it basic — so it is the trap, not the answer. 7 is the value for pure water; adding even a trace of a strong acid must push the hydronium concentration above \(10^{-7}\), so the pH must fall below 7, never stay at 7. "Greater than 7" fails for the same reason. The section on acidity and basicity of aqueous solutions states that in an acidic solution \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] > 1 \times 10^{-7}\) and pH \(< 7\), which is exactly the condition here.

pH \(= 1.0\) means \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = 10^{-1} = 0.1\) mol dm\(^{-3}\). \(\mathrm{HCl}\) and \(\mathrm{NaOH}\) are both strong electrolytes, so the excess of one after neutralisation fixes the pH. Millimoles are volume (mL) \(\times\) molarity, and the total volume is the sum of the two volumes.

Option D: \(\mathrm{HCl} = 75 \times 0.2 = 15\) mmol, \(\mathrm{NaOH} = 25 \times 0.2 = 5\) mmol, excess acid \(= 10\) mmol in 100 mL, so \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = 0.1\) M and pH \(= 1.00\).

Testing the other three: in A the acid and base are 5 mmol each, so neutralisation is exact and the solution is neutral, pH 7. In B the excess acid is \(6 - 4 = 2\) mmol in 100 mL \(= 0.02\) M, giving pH \(= 1.70\). In C the base is in excess by \(8 - 2 = 6\) mmol in 100 mL \(= 0.06\) M, so pOH \(= 1.22\) and pH \(= 12.78\) — an alkaline solution. Only D gives 1.0.

The chapter defines an acidic buffer as a solution containing a WEAK ACID and its SALT WITH A STRONG BASE, and a basic buffer as a weak base with its salt of a strong acid. A buffer must therefore hold a weak electrolyte and its conjugate partner together, in comparable amounts.

Option C is \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) (weak acid) together with \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\) (its salt with the strong base \(\mathrm{NaOH}\)) — precisely the acidic buffer the chapter uses as its worked example of buffer action. The large reservoir of \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}}\) mops up added \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), while the large reservoir of undissociated \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) neutralises added \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\).

Testing the others: A pairs \(\mathrm{CH_3COONa}\) with \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) — two salts and no weak acid at all, so nothing can consume added \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\). B pairs a weak acid with a STRONG acid; \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is not the conjugate partner of \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) and in fact suppresses its ionisation by the common ion effect, leaving no appreciable \(\mathrm{CH_3COO^{\ominus}}\) reservoir. D pairs a strong acid with \(\mathrm{NH_4Cl}\), the salt of a weak base, but the weak base \(\mathrm{NH_4OH}\) itself is absent. Only C is a buffer.

For the sparingly soluble salt AX the solubility equilibrium is \(\mathrm{AX(s)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{A^{\oplus}(aq)} + \mathrm{X^{\ominus}(aq)}\), so \(x = 1\) and \(y = 1\) and the solubility product is \(K_{sp} = [\mathrm{A^{\oplus}}][\mathrm{X^{\ominus}}] = S \times S = S^2\).

Hence \(S = \sqrt{K_{sp}} = \sqrt{5.2 \times 10^{-13}} = 7.2 \times 10^{-7}\) mol dm\(^{-3}\), which is option A.

Testing the others by squaring them back: \((1.35 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-8}\), \((7.2 \times 10^{-8})^2 = 5.2 \times 10^{-15}\) and \((13.5 \times 10^{-8})^2 = 1.8 \times 10^{-14}\) — none of them returns \(5.2 \times 10^{-13}\), so each is excluded. Note that \(1.35 \times 10^{-4}\) is the distractor to watch: it is the MASS solubility in g dm\(^{-3}\) of the salt in the chapter's worked example with the same \(K_{sp}\), not a molar solubility, and the question asks for mol dm\(^{-3}\).

The chapter states in its applications of buffer solutions that the pH of blood in our body is maintained at 7.36 to 7.42 by the \((\mathrm{HCO_3^{\ominus}} + \mathrm{H_2CO_3})\) buffer, and adds that a change of only 0.2 pH units can cause death. The same figure appears in the chapter's "Do you know?" note.

Of the four options only 7.4 lies inside that range, so A is the answer.

Testing the others against the printed range: 7.0 is 0.36 below the lower limit, 6.9 is 0.46 below it, and 8.1 is 0.68 above the upper limit — every one of them is outside the stated band by more than the 0.2 units the chapter says is fatal. Note also that blood is slightly alkaline, which rules out the two acidic values on the list independently.

On the Bronsted-Lowry definition the chapter gives, the conjugate base of an acid is the species left after that acid RELEASES ONE PROTON. So the answer must be \([\mathrm{Zn(H_2O)_4}]^{2\oplus}\) minus one \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\): one of the four coordinated water molecules loses a hydrogen and becomes a hydroxide, and the overall charge falls by one unit from \(2\oplus\) to \(\oplus\).

That gives \([\mathrm{Zn(H_2O)_3OH}]^{\oplus}\) — option C. It has the correct atom count (three intact waters plus one \(\mathrm{OH}\) accounts for the original four oxygens and one fewer hydrogen) and the correct charge.

Testing the others: A has GAINED an \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) that appears nowhere in the parent ion and carries the wrong sign of charge; a conjugate base cannot acquire a new ligand. B has lost a whole water molecule rather than a proton, and its charge of \(2\ominus\) differs from the parent by four units instead of one. D has lost three waters and its charge has gone UP to \(3\oplus\), which is the direction an acid moves when it ACCEPTS a proton, not when it donates one. Only C is one proton away from the parent ion.

By definition pH \(= -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}]\), so the hydronium concentration is \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}\). Because of the minus sign the relation is inverse: the larger the pH, the SMALLER the hydronium concentration.

If pH \(> 7\) then \(-\mathrm{pH} < -7\), so \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] < 10^{-7}\) M. For instance pH 8 gives \(10^{-8}\) M, a tenth of the neutral value. This is exactly what the chapter states for a basic solution: \([\mathrm{H_3O^{\oplus}}] < 1.0 \times 10^{-7}\) with pH \(> 7\).

Testing the others: \(10^{-7}\) M is the value at pH exactly 7 and the question excludes that point; \(> 10^{-7}\) M is the acidic case, pH \(< 7\), the opposite of what is asked; and \(\geq 10^{-7}\) M admits both the neutral point and the whole acidic range, so it is false for every solution the question describes. Only B holds.
